title: Dizziness and Vertigo Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for classifying dizziness by timing and triggers, recognising central and cardiovascular causes, performing focused vestibular, neurological and postural examination, and selecting an appropriate referral or community pathway.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: First define the syndrome: continuous acute vestibular symptoms, brief triggered episodes, spontaneous episodes, presyncope or nonspecific imbalance. Do not use the word dizziness as a diagnosis.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Exact timing, duration, frequency and triggers rather than relying only on the patient’s descriptive word.
Sudden-onset acute vestibular syndrome: continuous vertigo or dizziness with nausea or vomiting, spontaneous nystagmus and gait unsteadiness.
Focal neurological symptoms, severe gait or truncal ataxia, new headache or neck pain, or other features of posterior circulation stroke.
Presyncope, syncope, arrhythmia, bleeding, hypoglycaemia, postural hypotension or medication effect.
Hearing loss, tinnitus, ear pain or neurological symptoms that change the differential and urgency.
Whether HINTS or positional testing is appropriate, safe and within the clinician’s training and governance.
Baseline gait, current ability to stand and walk, and whether discharge is functionally safe.
items.importantLimitation: Normal FAST findings do not exclude posterior circulation stroke. HINTS should not be used for intermittent dizziness, isolated presyncope, a patient without spontaneous nystagmus, or by an untrained clinician.

sections.title: History prompts
sections.intro: Classify the presentation using timing, triggers and targeted associated symptoms.

items.title: Timing and triggers
mustConfirmOrExclude: Sudden or gradual onset and exact time last known well.
Continuous symptoms lasting hours or days versus discrete episodes with complete or partial recovery.
Episode duration: seconds, minutes, hours or longer.
Triggered by rolling in bed, looking up, bending, standing or exertion, or occurring spontaneously.
Whether movement triggers a new brief episode or merely worsens continuous symptoms already present.
First episode or recurrent stereotyped episodes.

items.title: What the patient experiences
mustConfirmOrExclude: Illusion of movement or spinning, light-headedness, impending faint, imbalance, visual motion or nonspecific weakness.
Nausea, vomiting and ability to retain fluids.
Oscillopsia or blurred vision during head movement.
Severity at rest and with movement.
Effect on standing, walking, transfers, driving and self-care.

items.title: Neurological and central-cause screen
mustConfirmOrExclude: Diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, facial weakness or numbness.
Limb weakness, numbness, incoordination or new clumsiness.
Severe gait or truncal unsteadiness, falls or inability to stand unaided.
New severe headache, occipital headache or neck pain.
Reduced consciousness, seizure or recent head and neck trauma.
Previous stroke or TIA and vascular risk factors.

items.title: Ear and hearing symptoms
mustConfirmOrExclude: New unilateral or bilateral hearing loss.
Tinnitus, aural fullness, ear pain or discharge.
Recent viral illness or otological procedure.
Recurrent episodes associated with fluctuating hearing symptoms.
Use of hearing aids and baseline hearing impairment.

items.title: Presyncope, cardiac and postural symptoms
mustConfirmOrExclude: Symptoms occurring on standing, after prolonged standing, after meals or with dehydration.
Palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, exertional symptoms or true loss of consciousness.
Bleeding, vomiting, diarrhoea, poor intake or recent illness.
Known arrhythmia, structural heart disease or family history of sudden cardiac death.
Falls with uncertain loss of consciousness.

items.title: Migraine and recurrent episodic symptoms
mustConfirmOrExclude: Current or previous migraine, photophobia, phonophobia, aura or headache.
Recurrent stereotyped vertigo lasting minutes to hours.
Motion sensitivity and visual triggers.
Neurological symptoms that might represent TIA rather than migraine.
Whether the pattern has changed from previous episodes.

items.title: Medicines and substances
mustConfirmOrExclude: Recent start or dose change of antihypertensives, diuretics, sedatives, anticonvulsants, antidepressants or ototoxic medicines.
Alcohol, recreational drugs or possible overdose.
Hypoglycaemic medicines and timing of food intake.
Polypharmacy, renal impairment and risk of medicine accumulation.
Recent medication non-adherence or abrupt withdrawal.

sections.title: Central, cardiovascular and urgent-cause screen
sections.intro: Use JRCALC and local emergency pathways when a time-critical cause is suspected. This guide supports recognition and disposition rather than duplicating emergency treatment.

items.title: Posterior circulation stroke
urgentFeatures: Sudden-onset acute vestibular syndrome not explained by benign positional vertigo or postural hypotension.
Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation on a correctly performed HINTS examination.
New focal neurological deficit, severe gait or truncal ataxia, inability to stand, dysarthria, diplopia or dysphagia.
New severe headache or neck pain, especially with neurological symptoms.
implications: Immediate referral through the local stroke pathway.
items.importantLimitation: A patient can have posterior circulation stroke without facial weakness, arm weakness or speech disturbance.

items.title: Acute vestibular syndrome without trained HINTS assessment
urgentFeatures: Continuous sudden-onset vertigo or dizziness with nausea or vomiting and gait unsteadiness.
No clear benign positional or postural explanation.
No clinician with training and experience in HINTS is available.
implications: Refer immediately in line with the local stroke pathway.

items.title: Syncope, arrhythmia or haemodynamic cause
urgentFeatures: True loss of consciousness, exertional presyncope, chest pain or palpitations.
Persistent hypotension, significant bradycardia or tachyarrhythmia.
Abnormal ECG, active bleeding or severe volume depletion.
Family history of sudden death or known high-risk structural heart disease.
implications: Use the syncope or cardiac pathway rather than diagnosing peripheral vertigo.

items.title: Acute hearing loss with vertigo
urgentFeatures: Sudden new hearing loss, particularly unilateral, with vertigo or neurological symptoms.
Ear symptoms do not fully explain severe gait or neurological abnormality.
implications: Requires urgent specialist assessment; new hearing loss does not automatically establish a benign peripheral cause.

items.title: Unsafe mobility or uncontrolled symptoms
urgentFeatures: Unable to stand, walk or transfer safely.
Persistent vomiting with inability to retain fluids or medicines.
Repeated falls, injury or no safe supervision at home.
implications: Disposition must address function, hydration and support even if a peripheral vestibular diagnosis appears likely.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Select tests according to the syndrome. Do not perform every vestibular manoeuvre on every patient.

items.title: General assessment and observations
howToTest: Assess appearance, distress, hydration and ability to engage.
Record temperature, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and glucose.
Review symptom onset and any change during observation.
Assess vomiting and ability to retain oral fluids.
normal: Physiologically stable with normal glucose and controlled symptoms.
abnormal: Hypotension, arrhythmia, fever, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia or persistent vomiting.
implications: May identify a metabolic, infectious, cardiovascular or volume-related cause rather than a primary vestibular disorder.

items.title: Eye movements and spontaneous nystagmus
howToTest: Inspect primary gaze and gaze to each side without asking the patient to fix on a near target.
Assess whether nystagmus is unidirectional or changes direction with gaze.
Assess ocular alignment and full eye movements.
Look for new diplopia, gaze palsy or vertical nystagmus.
normal: Full conjugate eye movements and no spontaneous nystagmus.
abnormal: Direction-changing, vertical or pure torsional nystagmus.
Skew deviation, gaze palsy or new diplopia.
Unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus in an appropriate acute vestibular syndrome.
implications: Direction-changing nystagmus, skew or other ocular motor abnormality raises concern for a central cause.

items.title: HINTS examination in acute vestibular syndrome
items.summary: Use only for continuous acute vestibular syndrome with spontaneous nystagmus, and only when trained and experienced.
howToTest: Head impulse: assess the vestibulo-ocular reflex with small rapid head turns while the patient fixes on a target.
Nystagmus: determine whether it remains unidirectional or changes direction with gaze.
Test of skew: perform alternate cover testing and observe for vertical corrective movement.
Interpret the three components together and document each component, not simply HINTS negative or positive.
normal: A peripheral pattern may include an abnormal unilateral head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus and no skew.
abnormal: Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation indicates a central pattern.
implications: A central HINTS pattern requires immediate neuroimaging and stroke referral.
When trained HINTS assessment is unavailable and benign positional vertigo or postural hypotension does not explain acute vestibular syndrome, refer immediately.
urgentFeatures: Normal head impulse in acute vestibular syndrome.
items.importantLimitation: Do not use HINTS in brief triggered episodes, isolated imbalance, presyncope, a patient without spontaneous nystagmus or a patient whose symptoms have resolved.

items.title: Dix-Hallpike positional test
howToTest: Use when the history suggests brief rotational vertigo triggered by head position and there is no contraindication to the manoeuvre.
Explain the test and obtain consent.
Turn the head approximately 45 degrees and move the patient rapidly from sitting to a head-hanging position with support.
Observe the eyes and ask whether familiar vertigo is reproduced.
Test the other side after symptoms settle.
normal: No familiar vertigo and no characteristic positional nystagmus.
abnormal: Brief latency followed by transient positional vertigo with a characteristic torsional up-beating nystagmus for posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
implications: A compatible history and characteristic positional response support benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
items.importantLimitation: Avoid or modify the test when neck movement is unsafe. Persistent, atypical or purely vertical nystagmus should prompt reconsideration of a central cause.

items.title: Neurological and cerebellar examination
howToTest: Assess speech, facial movement, limb power and sensation.
Assess finger-nose testing, heel-shin testing and rapid alternating movements.
Assess visual fields and cranial nerves where indicated.
Look for limb dysmetria, truncal ataxia or a focal deficit.
normal: No focal neurological deficit or limb incoordination.
abnormal: Dysarthria, cranial nerve abnormality, weakness, sensory loss, dysmetria or truncal ataxia.
implications: Any new focal or cerebellar finding increases concern for central pathology and requires urgent stroke assessment.

items.title: Gait and truncal stability
howToTest: Observe sitting balance before standing.
Assess standing with support available and walk using the usual aid when safe.
Look for veering, broad-based gait, inability to take steps or severe truncal instability.
Compare with baseline gait and repeat after symptom treatment where appropriate.
normal: Able to sit, stand and walk close to baseline.
abnormal: Unable to sit unsupported, stand or walk; severe new veering; broad-based or markedly ataxic gait.
implications: Severe gait or truncal ataxia is concerning for a central cause and makes discharge unsafe even without another focal sign.

items.title: Lying and standing blood pressure
howToTest: Measure blood pressure lying down or seated if necessary.
Repeat after standing for at least 1 minute when safe.
Record symptoms, pulse response and the numerical change.
Repeat from lying if a seated baseline is inconclusive and symptoms remain suggestive.
normal: No significant fall and no postural symptoms.
abnormal: Systolic fall of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg after standing.
Reproduction of presyncope or postural dizziness.
implications: Review volume status, medications, autonomic causes and falls risk.
items.importantLimitation: A postural blood pressure fall does not exclude a simultaneous vestibular or neurological cause.

items.title: Cardiovascular examination and ECG
howToTest: Assess pulse rate and regularity and perform cardiovascular examination as indicated.
Obtain a 12-lead ECG when presyncope, syncope, palpitations, exertional symptoms or cardiac risk is present.
Assess for bleeding, dehydration and medicine-related hypotension.
normal: Regular pulse, stable blood pressure and no concerning ECG or cardiac symptoms.
abnormal: Arrhythmia, conduction abnormality, persistent hypotension, exertional symptoms or true loss of consciousness.
implications: Use the cardiac or syncope pathway rather than attributing symptoms to vertigo.

items.title: Hearing and ear examination
howToTest: Ask about and compare hearing between ears.
Use a simple bedside hearing comparison and otoscopy where appropriate and within scope.
Assess for ear pain, discharge, vesicles or mastoid features.
Document whether hearing loss is new or baseline.
normal: No new hearing asymmetry or acute ear findings.
abnormal: New unilateral hearing loss, ear vesicles, significant otalgia, discharge or mastoid signs.
implications: New hearing loss changes the differential and may require urgent ENT or stroke assessment depending on associated findings.

sections.title: Common clinical patterns
sections.intro: Patterns should emerge from timing, triggers and examination together. A symptom label alone is insufficient.

items.title: Posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
commonFindings: Brief episodes, usually seconds, triggered by rolling in bed, looking up or another head-position change.
The patient is usually relatively well between episodes, although mild disequilibrium may persist.
Dix-Hallpike reproduces familiar vertigo with characteristic transient torsional up-beating nystagmus.
Neurological examination and gait are otherwise reassuring.
implications: Supports BPPV and a locally governed canalith-repositioning and follow-up pathway.

keyTriggers: Image only when the history or examination is atypical or a central cause is suspected.
guidance: Do not routinely arrange neuroimaging for a characteristic BPPV presentation without central features.

items.importantLimitation: Head movement also worsens many central and peripheral vestibular disorders; the brief triggered pattern and characteristic positional nystagmus are important.

items.title: Likely vestibular neuritis
commonFindings: Continuous acute vestibular syndrome lasting hours to days.
Nausea, vomiting, unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus and gait unsteadiness.
No new hearing loss or focal neurological deficit.
A trained HINTS examination shows a peripheral pattern.
implications: Supports a peripheral vestibular cause only after central features have been actively assessed.
items.importantLimitation: Do not diagnose vestibular neuritis solely because the patient has vertigo and vomiting.

items.title: Peripheral vestibular syndrome with hearing symptoms
commonFindings: Acute continuous vertigo with new hearing loss or tinnitus.
No focal neurological deficit and no central HINTS pattern when assessed by a trained clinician.
Possible recent viral illness.
implications: Consider labyrinthitis or another audiovestibular disorder, but arrange urgent assessment for sudden hearing loss and reconsider stroke when central features are present.

items.title: Recurrent episodic vertigo with auditory symptoms
commonFindings: Recurrent spontaneous episodes lasting minutes to hours.
Fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus or aural fullness.
Neurological examination is normal between attacks.
implications: Supports an audiovestibular referral pathway after urgent neurological and cardiac causes have been excluded.

items.title: Possible vestibular migraine
commonFindings: Recurrent episodes with migraine history, photophobia, phonophobia, aura or migrainous headache.
Symptoms may be spontaneous or visually triggered.
No persistent focal neurological deficit.
implications: Consider after excluding stroke or TIA in a new, atypical or high-risk presentation.
items.importantLimitation: A history of migraine does not protect against stroke.

items.title: Postural dizziness or presyncope
commonFindings: Light-headedness or impending faint on standing rather than a clear illusion of movement.
Systolic blood pressure fall of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic fall of at least 10 mmHg after standing.
Medication, volume loss, autonomic dysfunction or deconditioning may contribute.
implications: Review causes, medication and falls risk; use standing blood pressure for subsequent management where relevant.

items.title: Possible cardiac presyncope or syncope
commonFindings: Impending faint, true loss of consciousness, palpitations or exertional symptoms.
Abnormal pulse, ECG or structural cardiac history.
No characteristic positional vertigo or vestibular examination pattern.
implications: Use the cardiac or transient-loss-of-consciousness pathway.

items.title: Possible central vestibular syndrome
commonFindings: Sudden continuous vestibular symptoms with severe gait or truncal ataxia.
Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew on trained HINTS assessment.
Focal neurological signs, new severe headache or neck pain may be present but can be absent.
implications: Immediate stroke referral and neuroimaging through the receiving-hospital pathway.

preferredImaging: Urgent brain and vascular imaging through the local stroke pathway.
keyTriggers: Acute vestibular syndrome without a trained HINTS assessor and no benign positional or postural explanation.
guidance: Refer immediately through the local stroke pathway; do not delay referral for routine community imaging.

items.title: Medication or metabolic dizziness
commonFindings: Temporal relationship to a medicine change, polypharmacy, renal impairment, alcohol or another substance.
Sedation, postural hypotension, hypoglycaemia or diffuse imbalance without a focal vestibular pattern.
Symptoms improve when the cause is corrected.
implications: Treat the metabolic cause and arrange medication review, while excluding simultaneous neurological or cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Potentially suitable for community management
commonFindings: A coherent benign diagnosis supported by the timing, triggers and examination.
No central, cardiac or serious metabolic features.
Symptoms are controlled and the person can stand, walk, eat, drink and self-care safely.
Reliable supervision, follow-up and return precautions are available.
implications: Document why central and cardiovascular alternatives are less likely, the functional assessment, treatment response and follow-up plan.
items.importantLimitation: A benign diagnostic label does not make discharge safe when the patient remains unable to walk or retain fluids.

sections.title: Focused safety-netting
sections.intro: Provide advice matching the suspected syndrome and functional risk.

items.title: Dizziness or vertigo
safetyNetting: Call 999 for any significant deterioration, including difficulty breathing, chest pain, collapse, reduced consciousness or any immediate concern.

Seek urgent reassessment for new weakness or numbness; facial droop; speech, swallowing or vision change; a new severe headache or neck pain; inability to stand or walk; repeated vomiting or inability to drink; new hearing loss; fainting or palpitations; or symptoms that become continuous, markedly worse or different from the assessed pattern.
Avoid driving, working at height or operating machinery while symptoms could impair balance or concentration. Follow the agreed review and vestibular, falls, cardiac or stroke pathway.
items.importantLimitation: Safety-netting does not make discharge appropriate when posterior circulation stroke, arrhythmia or unsafe mobility has not been adequately addressed.
